propositions.text: Applicant seeks judicial review of IAD decision allowing Ministers' appeal and issuing deportation order.
propositions.quote: Mr. Monday Iyangbe Eriator (the Applicant) seeks the judicial review of a decision of the Immigration Appeal Division (IAD) which allowed the appeal of the Ministers.

propositions.text: ID found Applicant not inadmissible; IAD allowed Ministers' appeal and issued deportation order.
propositions.quote: The Immigration Division (ID) had found Mr. Eriator not inadmissible. The Ministers appealed and a panel of the IAD allowed the appeal and issued a deportation order.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant seeks judicial review of IAD decision allowing Ministers' appeal; ID found Applicant not inadmissible, IAD issued deportation order.

propositions.text: Judicial review authorized under section 72 IRPA; application must be granted due to unreasonableness of impugned decision.
propositions.quote: The judicial review application was authorized pursuant to section 72 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, SC 2001, c 27 [the Act or IRPA]. The application must be granted.

propositions.text: Reasonableness requires justification, transparency, intelligibility, and coherence per Vavilov.
propositions.quote: The impugned decision is not reasonable in that it does not bear “the hallmarks of reasonableness — justification, transparency and intelligibility — and whether it is justified in relation to the relevant factual and legal constraints that bear on the decision” (Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration) v Vavilov, 2019 SCC 65 at para 99 [Vavilov]).

propositions.text: Decision must have internally coherent reasoning without logical fallacies per Vavilov.
propositions.quote: A decision must be based on an internally coherent reasoning. As the Supreme Court noted in Vavilov: [104] Similarly, the internal rationality of a decision may be called into question if the reasons exhibit clear logical fallacies, such as circular reasoning, false dilemmas, unfounded generalizations or an absurd premise.

propositions.text: Impugned decision lacks internal rationality and is unreasonable.
propositions.quote: The decision under review suffers from a lack of internal rationality.

paragraphs.summary: Court grants judicial review under IRPA section 72, finds impugned decision unreasonable and lacking internal rationality per Vavilov.

propositions.text: Applicant is Nigerian born 1979, crossed US-Canada border irregularly in 2017, not citizen or permanent resident, refugee claim in abeyance due to alleged inadmissibility.
propositions.quote: The Applicant is a Nigerian national born in 1979. He crossed the border between Canada and the United States between ports of entry (through Roxham Rd) on October 23, 2017. He is neither a Canada citizen nor a permanent resident of this country. He claimed refugee protection but his claim is in abeyance as it was alleged that he is inadmissible to Canada.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant is Nigerian, crossed irregularly in 2017, refugee claim in abeyance due to alleged inadmissibility.

propositions.text: Applicant subject to report under section 44(1) IRPA for inadmissibility hearing alleging offences under Crimes Against Humanity and War Crimes Act.
propositions.quote: Mr. Eriator was made the subject of a report made pursuant to section 44(1) of the Act on July 3, 2018. The report was referred to the ID for an inadmissibility hearing. It is alleged that Mr. Eriator is inadmissible pursuant to paragraph 35(1)(a) of the Act, which reads: Human or international rights violations...

paragraphs.summary: Applicant reported under IRPA section 44(1) for inadmissibility hearing alleging offences under Crimes Against Humanity and War Crimes Act.

propositions.text: Applicant was Nigerian Police Force member from 2009 to 2016 with various roles including SARS assignment in December 2016.
propositions.quote: The allegation relates to the uncontested fact that the Applicant was a member of the Nigerian Police Force (NPF). He joined the Force voluntarily in June 2009 and left on December 31, 2016. His employment with the NPF is presented as follows: Clerical officer... Assigned to the Special Anti-Robbery Squad (SARS) in Ikeja from December 5, 2016 to December 10, 2016.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant was Nigerian Police Force member 2009-2016 with various roles including SARS assignment in December 2016.

propositions.text: Little known about Applicant's departure from Nigeria and arrival in Canada except he came from US and crossed border irregularly.
propositions.quote: Very little is known about the circumstances surrounding the Applicant’s departure from Nigeria and his arrival in Canada in October 2017. The only thing that is known is that he came from the United States and he crossed the border at a place other than a port of entry.

paragraphs.summary: Little known about Applicant's departure from Nigeria and arrival in Canada except irregular border crossing from US.

propositions.text: Inadmissibility allegation based on complicity in crimes by Nigerian Police Force; various human rights reports submitted as evidence.
propositions.quote: The allegation that the Applicant is inadmissible by reason of committing outside of Canada offences referred to in sections 4 to 7 of the Crimes Against Humanity and War Crimes Act relates to his service in the NPF. As will become apparent, the allegation is based on complicity in crimes committed during his career by the NPF. Documentary evidence was submitted which reports on offences perpetrated in Nigeria.

paragraphs.summary: Allegation of inadmissibility based on complicity in crimes by Nigerian Police Force; human rights reports submitted.

propositions.text: ID panel referred to reports documenting corruption and torture in Nigerian Police, including SARS and CID use of torture chambers.
propositions.quote: The ID panel referred to a number of paragraphs taken from these publications. They are generally of a generic nature and tend to document that corruption on a significant scale is present in Nigeria. Torture is mentioned frequently... Amnesty International found that torture is such a routine and systemic part of policy that many police sections... use designated ‘torture chamber’: special interrogation rooms commonly used for torturing suspects.

propositions.text: Open Society Institute reports SARS and SCIDs responsible for extrajudicial executions.
propositions.quote: The Open Society Institute New York (2010) speaks of SARS and State Criminal Investigation Divisions (SCIDs) as widely believed to be responsible for extrajudicial executions.

paragraphs.summary: ID panel cited reports documenting Nigerian Police corruption, torture, and SARS involvement in extrajudicial executions.

propositions.text: Amnesty International 2016 report details SARS background, methods, detention center conditions, and impunity due to bribery.
propositions.quote: It is the Amnesty International report of 2016 which is most specific on the activities of SARS units. I reproduce a number of paragraphs the ID panel had in its reasons: page 731 SARS: BACKGROUND AND WORKING METHODS...

paragraphs.summary: Amnesty International 2016 report details SARS background, detention center, and impunity due to bribery, cited by ID panel.

propositions.text: ID and IAD reasons do not specify number of SARS units or officers; no evidence of Applicant's involvement beyond his testimony.
propositions.quote: The ID division notes that there were, in 2009, 377,000 members of the NPF. I have not found in the reasons of the ID or the IAD how many SARS units there are... There was not either any evidence of the involvement of the Applicant in the police activities other than what he testified to.

paragraphs.summary: ID and IAD did not specify SARS numbers; no evidence of Applicant's involvement beyond his testimony.

propositions.text: Ministers relied on Applicant's contribution to crimes and criminal purpose of NPF, not specific crime participation; crimes identified as crimes against humanity.
propositions.quote: The Ministers never relied on some evidence that the Applicant participated in any specific crime. Rather they relied exclusively on the contribution that the Applicant made to the crimes and the criminal purpose of the organization... The crimes identified were not genocide nor war crime, but rather crimes against humanity.

propositions.text: Definition of crime against humanity per Crimes Against Humanity and War Crimes Act provided.
propositions.quote: It is defined as follows in the Crimes Against Humanity and War Crimes Act, SC 2000, c 24: crime against humanity means murder, extermination, enslavement, deportation, imprisonment, torture, sexual violence, persecution or any other inhumane act or omission...

paragraphs.summary: Ministers relied on Applicant's contribution to crimes against humanity by NPF; definition of crime against humanity provided.

propositions.text: Ministers argued Applicant's complicity based on Nigerian policing context and his voluntary NPF membership and promotion.
propositions.quote: In an attempt to establish the level of contribution as required by the Supreme Court of Canada in Ezokola v Canada... the Minister referred to the state of policing in Nigeria... More specifically with respect to Mr. Eriator, the Ministers resorted to the fact that he joined the NPF voluntarily, that he was promoted from constable to corporal in 2014 and that the Applicant knew when he joined that the NPF had committed human rights violations.

propositions.text: Ministers raised credibility concerns about Applicant's career and knowledge of human rights violations, rejecting his denials.
propositions.quote: The Ministers also argued about what was referred to as “several credibility concerns” with regard to the Applicant’s career and his knowledge of human rights violation committed by the NPF. The Applicant was not to be believed when he stated he had not witnessed torture and that he was not aware of human rights violations.

paragraphs.summary: Ministers argued Applicant's complicity based on Nigerian policing context, voluntary NPF membership, promotion, and credibility concerns.

propositions.text: Ministers alleged Applicant was untruthful about being unarmed and recruitment testimony contradictions.
propositions.quote: Similarly, Mr. Eriator is not truthful when he claims that he was not armed during his posting as a security guard or when he was a member of SARS... The Ministers complained about the way the Applicant testified he was recruited in the NPF and suggest that there exists a contradiction.

paragraphs.summary: Ministers alleged Applicant was untruthful about being unarmed and recruitment testimony contradictions.

propositions.text: Applicant's counsel argued discrepancies due to interpretation errors and no significant contribution to crimes per Ezokola.
propositions.quote: Counsel for Mr. Eriator argued that some discrepancies in the Applicant’s testimony are due to interpretation errors. Fundamentally, counsel submitted that the Ezokola analysis led to an absence of complicity: there is no significant contribution to the group’s crimes. Mere association with an organization does not suffice.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant's counsel argued discrepancies due to interpretation errors and no significant contribution to crimes per Ezokola.

propositions.text: Applicant's SARS involvement was brief and low rank; awareness of violations does not equal complicity; Minister failed burden.
propositions.quote: The Applicant’s involvement with a SARS unit lasted less than one month... He was not unaware of the Force’s bad reputation, but being aware of events does not lead to complicity... the Minister has not presented any credible and trustworthy evidence to establish that there are reasonable grounds to believe that Mr. Eriator made a significant and knowing contribution to crimes...

paragraphs.summary: Applicant argued brief low-rank SARS involvement and awareness does not equal complicity; Minister failed burden.

propositions.text: ID found complicity in crimes against humanity not established; issue is grounds to believe offence under Crimes Against Humanity and War Crimes Act committed.
propositions.quote: After a careful analysis, the ID agreed with Mr. Eriator that complicity in the commission of crimes against humanity had not been established. As said explicitly, the issue is whether there are grounds to believe... that Mr. Eriator has committed an offence found in sections 4 to 7 of the Crimes Against Humanity and War Crimes Act.

paragraphs.summary: ID found complicity not established; issue is grounds to believe offence under Crimes Against Humanity and War Crimes Act committed.

propositions.text: ID applied Ezokola factors to assess significant and knowing contribution to crime or criminal purpose.
propositions.quote: Applying the Ezokola framework, the ID refers specifically to paragraphs 87, 88, 94 and 95. Thus, six factors that “serve as a guide in assessing whether an individual has voluntarily made a significant and knowing contribution to a crime or criminal purpose” (Ezokola, at para 91) are considered.

propositions.text: Six Ezokola factors: size/nature of organization; part claimant concerned with; duties; rank; length of time after knowledge; recruitment and opportunity to leave.
propositions.quote: They are: (i) the size and nature of the organization; (ii) the part of the organization with which the refugee claimant was most directly concerned; (iii) the refugee claimant’s duties and activities within the organization; (iv) the refugee claimant’s position or rank in the organization; (v) the length of time the refugee claimant was in the organization, particularly after acquiring knowledge of the group’s crime or criminal purpose; and (vi) the method by which the refugee claimant was recruited and the refugee claimant’s opportunity to leave the organization.

paragraphs.summary: ID applied Ezokola six-factor test to assess significant and knowing contribution to crime or criminal purpose.

propositions.text: ID found burden not satisfied that Applicant significantly contributed to crimes; Applicant did clerical work and occasional complaint investigations.
propositions.quote: The ID finds that the burden of establishing that the NPF, and in particular SARS, have committed crimes against humanity during Mr. Eriator’s career to which Mr. Eriator did contribute significantly has not been satisfied... the ID found a lack of “credible and trustworthy evidence to believe that Mr. Eriator did anything else than clerical work, except from time to time he would investigate complaints brought before him” (ID decision, para 44).

paragraphs.summary: ID found burden not met that Applicant significantly contributed to crimes; he did clerical work and occasional complaint investigations.

propositions.text: ID found Applicant's credibility negatively affected by implausible incident prompting his departure from SARS and NPF.
propositions.quote: Mr. Eriator’s credibility concerning the incident that, he says, prompted him to leave SARS, and the NPF altogether, had a negative effect on his credibility... The ID found “the incident generally implausible” (ID decision, para 50).

paragraphs.summary: ID found Applicant's credibility negatively affected by implausible incident prompting his departure from SARS and NPF.

propositions.text: Despite unanswered questions, ID found no clear evidence Applicant was involved in human rights violations during SARS posting; speculation rejected.
propositions.quote: In spite of finding the incident implausible, it remained, in the view of the ID panel, that there was an absence of evidence that Mr. Eriator was himself involved in crimes against humanity while with SARS: [51] Although the tribunal has many unanswered questions about the December 2016 incident, it nonetheless concludes there is an absence of any clear evidence that Mr. Eriator was an armed SARS officer involved in any human rights violations either individually or in complicity with others during his brief posting with the SARS. The tribunal cannot engage in speculation of what could have occurred while Mr. Eriator was a member of the SARS team.

paragraphs.summary: ID found no clear evidence Applicant involved in human rights violations during SARS posting; speculation rejected despite unanswered questions.

propositions.text: The ID applied Ezokola as articulated in Concepcion, requiring proof of significant contribution to an international crime, not just association.
propositions.quote: The panel purported to apply Ezokola as articulated by this Court in Concepcion v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2016 FC 544: [17] ... the test now requires proof of a significant contribution to an international crime.

propositions.text: The evidence must show a significant contribution to a crime or the organization's criminal purpose, not just a contribution to the organization.
propositions.quote: The evidence must show, at least, that the person made a significant contribution to a crime or the organization’s criminal purpose, not just a contribution to the organization.

paragraphs.summary: The ID applied Ezokola requiring proof of significant contribution to a crime, not mere association, as explained in Concepcion (earlier decision-maker).

propositions.text: The ID concluded no credible evidence showed the Applicant made a significant, voluntary, knowing contribution to the NPF's criminal purpose.
propositions.quote: The ID concluded that it did not have objective, credible and trustworthy evidence demonstrating reasonable grounds to believe that the Applicant performed duties that could be considered as a significant, voluntary and knowing contribution to the criminal purpose of the NPF, including the SARS.

paragraphs.summary: The ID found no credible evidence that the Applicant significantly contributed to the NPF's criminal purpose (earlier decision-maker).

propositions.text: The judicial review concerns the IAD decision after the Ministers' appeal, which disagreed with the ID's reasons.
propositions.quote: The matter being the subject of the judicial review application is of course the decision of the IAD after an appeal launched by the Ministers. The IAD disagreed with the ID.

propositions.text: The IAD's reasons differ significantly from those of the ID.
propositions.quote: The examination of the reasons for decision of the ID tend to show the significant difference with the reasons given by the IAD.

paragraphs.summary: The judicial review concerns the IAD decision which disagreed with the ID and gave significantly different reasons (court).

propositions.text: The appeal focused on the kind of contribution required under Ezokola to establish complicity.
propositions.quote: I note that the appeal was heard on the basis that the contentious issue on appeal was the presence of the kind of contribution required since Ezokola in order to reach a conclusion of complicity.

propositions.text: Counsel for Mr. Eriator argued the IAD improperly delved into credibility issues, contrary to party agreement to avoid a new hearing.
propositions.quote: Counsel for Mr. Eriator complained bitterly that, in fact, the IAD delved into credibility issues, contrary to the agreement reached between the parties to avoid holding a new hearing before the IAD.

propositions.text: The IAD stated it is contrary to natural justice to rely solely on written testimony to reassess credibility unfavorably.
propositions.quote: the statement made by the IAD according to which “that is contrary to natural justice to rely solely on written testimony to reassess the respondent’s credibility in an unfavourable way” (IAD decision, para 5)

propositions.text: It is unclear how the IAD used the ID's credibility findings; this affects decision quality but not reasonableness.
propositions.quote: it is less than clear what use was actually made of the “credibility findings” made by the ID. These concerns could however go to the quality of the decision made, its justification and its intelligibility.

propositions.text: There are more serious problems with the IAD decision that make it unreasonable.
propositions.quote: There are, in my estimation, even more serious problems with this decision that make it unreasonable.

paragraphs.summary: The appeal focused on Ezokola contribution; applicant argued improper credibility issues; court finds IAD's use of credibility unclear and decision unreasonable (court, applicant).

propositions.text: Vavilov requires reasonableness of both decision outcome and decision-making process.
propositions.quote: the Supreme Court, in Vavilov, reiterated that not only the outcome of a decision must be reasonable, but also the decision making process must also be reasonable

propositions.text: Reasonableness review focuses on the decision made, including reasoning and outcome, requiring an internally coherent and rational chain of analysis.
propositions.quote: the focus of reasonableness review must be on the decision actually made by the decision maker, including both the decision maker’s reasoning process and the outcome

propositions.text: The IAD decision is defective in reasoning and justification under Vavilov.
propositions.quote: That is in my view what is defective in this decision.

paragraphs.summary: Vavilov requires reasonableness of decision and process; IAD decision is defective in reasoning and justification (court).

propositions.text: IAD's reasons on Applicant's credibility are vague, elliptical, and lack transparency, undermining protection against arbitrariness.
propositions.quote: The paragraphs are elliptical; they do not explain, are vague and less than transparent.

propositions.text: Reasons are the primary mechanism to show administrative decisions are reasonable to parties and courts (Vavilov).
propositions.quote: the reasons “are the primary mechanism by which administrative decision makers show that their decisions are reasonable — both to the affected parties and to the reviewing courts” (at para 81).

paragraphs.summary: IAD's credibility reasons are vague and lack transparency, undermining arbitrariness protection; reasons are key to show reasonableness (court, prior authority).

propositions.text: IAD accused ID of lacking overall assessment of complicity factors, but ID's analysis was clear and cogent.
propositions.quote: the IAD accuses the ID of lacking in its “overall assessment of the analysis factors regarding complicity”. The IAD states that “the panel considers that the totality of the factors demonstrate complicity” (para 10). It was a surprising statement as the analysis conducted by the ID examined clearly the relevant factors and did not appear to suffer from a lack of cogency by reason of lack of overall assessment of the factors.

paragraphs.summary: IAD accused ID of lacking overall assessment, but ID's analysis was clear and cogent (court).

propositions.text: IAD assessed Ezokola factors but ignored their purpose to prevent guilt by association.
propositions.quote: The IAD proceeds to assess the Ezokola factors. It never even alludes to the “raison d’être” of these factors.

propositions.text: Ezokola requires significant contribution to crime or criminal purpose, not mere association, with awareness of conduct assisting crime.
propositions.quote: the individual must make a significant contribution to the crime or criminal purpose of a group. Not any contribution will do. The Court articulates the requirement in paragraphs 88 to 90: ...

propositions.text: Ezokola paragraphs 88-90 explain the mens rea and significant contribution requirements for complicity.
propositions.quote: [88] Given that contributions of almost every nature to a group could be characterized as furthering its criminal purpose, the degree of the contribution must be carefully assessed. ...

paragraphs.summary: IAD assessed Ezokola factors but ignored their purpose; Ezokola requires significant contribution and awareness to avoid guilt by association (court, earlier decision-maker, prior authority).

propositions.text: IAD's reasons do not go beyond association of Mr. Eriator with police force to show significant contribution.
propositions.quote: As I read the reasons, they do not go beyond the association of Mr. Eriator with the police force.

propositions.text: Awareness of crimes is distinct from awareness that conduct assists furtherance of crime; Ezokola prevents guilt by association.
propositions.quote: Awareness of the crimes is one thing; awareness that the conduct “will assist in the furtherance of the crime or criminal purpose” is another. Guilt by association is what is to be prevented by the application of the Ezokola framework.

paragraphs.summary: IAD's reasons do not show significant contribution beyond association; awareness of conduct assisting crime is required to avoid guilt by association (court).

propositions.text: IAD noted NPF size (375,000 members) and found police membership indicates contribution due to widespread criminality.
propositions.quote: The size of the organization was duly noted by the IAD, with upwards of 375,000 members strong. ... the panel found that “the NPF’s criminality is so widespread in the country that being a police officer in Nigeria is already an indication of a certain contribution” (para 26).

propositions.text: Mere membership or failure to dissociate does not establish complicity; Ezokola requires careful assessment of size and nature of organization.
propositions.quote: Mere membership or failure to dissociate from a multifaceted organization do not found complicity. ... The factor concerning the size of the organization would have required an explanation in view of paragraph 94 of Ezokola. None was given: [94] The size and nature of the organization...

paragraphs.summary: IAD found police membership indicates contribution due to widespread criminality, but mere membership does not establish complicity; Ezokola requires careful assessment (court).

propositions.text: Applicant did clerical work and participated in many investigations; IAD linked investigations to torture without evidence.
propositions.quote: The IAD noted that while Mr. Eriator was involved in clerical work for most of his service, he nonetheless participated in investigations ... In Nigeria, investigations and torture are associated…

propositions.text: IAD concluded Applicant contributed to crimes by presence and duration without showing how this constitutes significant contribution.
propositions.quote: the panel found that “the respondent contributed in his own way to the crimes against humanity perpetrated by the organization ... There is no indication of what is meant by “in his own way”.

propositions.text: IAD's conclusion approaches guilt by association, lacking evidence of specific significant contribution.
propositions.quote: We are dangerously close to guilt by association, for being a member of an organization of 377,000 members.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant's clerical and investigative work linked to torture without evidence; IAD's conclusion approaches guilt by association without showing significant contribution (court).

propositions.text: Applicant participated in election control checks; no evidence he engaged in extortion or that all checkpoints involved extortion.
propositions.quote: there is no evidence that the Applicant took part in extortion when he helped man some checkpoints at election time. There is no evidence either that would suggest that every checkpoint is used for extortion.

propositions.text: IAD failed to explain how local extortion contributes significantly to crimes against humanity or criminal purpose.
propositions.quote: it is not explained how that kind of local extortion becomes a crime against humanity or contributes significantly to crimes against humanity or the criminal purpose of the organization.

propositions.text: Vavilov requires decisions to avoid logical fallacies such as unfounded generalizations.
propositions.quote: In Vavilov, the Court finds that “the internal rationality of a decision may be called into question if the reasons exhibit clear logical fallacies, such as ... unfounded generalizations ...” (at para 104).

propositions.text: IAD's reasoning about Applicant's presence reinforcing extortion system is an unfounded generalization and illogical.
propositions.quote: In my view such is the case here.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant's election checkpoint participation lacks evidence of extortion; IAD's reasoning is an unfounded generalization violating Vavilov (court, prior authority).

propositions.text: Applicant participated in SARS unit less than one month; no evidence about this particular unit's activities.
propositions.quote: There is absolutely no evidence that is offered by the IAD with respect to the particular unit joined by the Applicant in early December 2016.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant's brief SARS unit participation lacks evidence about that unit's activities (court).

propositions.text: Gunfight incident on Dec 23, 2016 deemed implausible by ID; no evidence SARS unit committed crimes during Applicant's membership.
propositions.quote: The incident on December 23, 2016 which involved a gunfight was seen as implausible by the ID. ... I have not found ... any indication of crimes that would have been committed by the SARS unit which the Applicant joined for less than one month.

propositions.text: IAD's conclusion that Applicant contributed to crimes during SARS membership is an unfounded generalization based on suspicion and lack of credibility.
propositions.quote: there are reasonable grounds to believe that the respondent contributed to the crimes committed by this unit during the very busy month that he worked ... This constitutes an unfounded generalization not supported by anything other than suppositions.

propositions.text: IAD's use of lack of credibility to support positive evidence of crimes is incoherent and unreasonable under Vavilov.
propositions.quote: it is rather incoherent that the lack of credibility making an incident implausible is taken as positive evidence of the commission of crimes against humanity.

paragraphs.summary: Gunfight incident implausible; IAD's conclusion of Applicant's contribution to SARS crimes is unfounded, incoherent, and unreasonable (court).

propositions.text: IAD's reasoning is circular and incoherent, discounting short duration but concluding significant contribution without evidence.
propositions.quote: While the duration is a factor ... the IAD finds that the factor is irrelevant because it has already concluded about the significant contribution.

propositions.text: IAD's conclusion that Applicant's presence ensured detention facility safety lacks explanation of contribution to crime.
propositions.quote: the panel nevertheless concludes that the mere presence at the police station helped ensure the safety of the detention facility. There is no indication how that contributes.

paragraphs.summary: IAD's reasoning is circular and incoherent, discounting short duration but concluding contribution; presence ensuring safety unexplained (court).

propositions.text: Ezokola states duties and rank indicate day-to-day participation and likelihood of knowledge of criminal purpose.
propositions.quote: The Ezokola Court found that the duties and activities within the organization are likely to be significant because they speak of the day-to-day participation in the activities of the organization. Similarly, the higher the rank the more likely the person knows of the organization’s crime or criminal purpose.

paragraphs.summary: Ezokola states duties and rank indicate participation and knowledge of criminal purpose (prior authority).

propositions.text: IAD emphasized Applicant's corporal rank, but rank is low and many corporals exist; no evidence supports control or knowledge claims.
propositions.quote: the panel tried to make hay out of the fact that Mr. Eriator made it to corporal in 2014. But the rank of corporal is the second lowest ... There is nothing to support such gratuitous observation.

paragraphs.summary: IAD emphasized Applicant's low corporal rank without evidence of control or knowledge (court).

propositions.text: After review, the IAD decision is not reasonable as it lacks appropriate decision-making process and justification.
propositions.quote: the Court can only conclude that the decision is not reasonable. In order to be reasonable, a decision needs to follow an appropriate decision-making process.

paragraphs.summary: The IAD decision is unreasonable due to lack of proper decision-making process and justification (court).

propositions.text: The IAD decision lacks intelligibility and fails to show how Ezokola framework was applied beyond mere association.
propositions.quote: the decision under review lacks intelligibility. The very reason for the Ezokola framework is to prevent against resorting to guilt by association. The reader does not know ... how the decision maker went from mere association ... to being complicit.

propositions.text: Decision maker must show significant contribution, not rely on mere presence; suspicions are insufficient.
propositions.quote: Ultimately, the decision maker must be able to show what the significant contribution is, as opposed to relying on the mere presence in the organization. Suspicions are not enough.

paragraphs.summary: IAD decision lacks intelligibility and fails to show significant contribution beyond association; suspicions insufficient (court).

propositions.text: No reasonable grounds exist to believe Applicant was complicit under Ezokola; decision is unreasonable under Vavilov.
propositions.quote: It has not been demonstrated ... that there are reasonable grounds to believe that Mr. Eriator has been complicit ... The decision is unreasonable within the meaning of Vavilov.

paragraphs.summary: No reasonable grounds show Applicant's complicity under Ezokola; decision is unreasonable under Vavilov (court).

propositions.text: The judicial review application is granted.
propositions.quote: As a result, the judicial review application is granted.

propositions.text: The parties did not suggest any question for certification pursuant to section 74 of the Act.
propositions.quote: The parties did not suggest any question for certification pursuant to section 74 of the Act.

propositions.text: The matter of the appeal is returned to a differently constituted panel of the Immigration Appeal Division for a new determination.
propositions.quote: The matter of the appeal of the decision of the Immigration Division is returned to a differently constituted panel of the Immigration Appeal Division for a new determination.

propositions.text: There is no question for certification.
propositions.quote: There is no question for certification.

paragraphs.summary: The court grants the judicial review application, returns the appeal to a new IAD panel, finds no certification question, and notes parties made no certification suggestion.
